summary: Sets out conventions for using the Session Description Protocol to describe ATM bearer connections and their adaptation layers. It covers AAL types 1, 2, and 5. It extends the use of SDP from RFC 2327 into telephony and ATM networks.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a shared form for describing a phone-call line on an old kind of network, so both ends agree how to talk.

questions: how does sdp describe an atm connection
subtitle: How to describe an ATM bearer connection, and the adaptation layer on it, using ordinary SDP lines.

tldr.problem: Gateways and call controllers using Megaco, SIP or MGCP needed a standard way to say which ATM connection should carry a voice, video or data call, and how it is adapted, without inventing a new description language.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3108 reuses the Session Description Protocol syntax from RFC 2327. It sets the network type to ATM, gives ATM-specific values to the address, session and media lines, and defines new media attributes for AAL types 1, 2 and 5.
tldr.outcome: The result is a long, exhaustive catalogue of conventions from which each application picks the subset it needs. It remains a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 3108 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It stays the reference for describing ATM bearer connections in SDP, though it applies only where the network type is ATM.

sections.title: What the Conventions Are For
sections.content:
SDP is used together with a connection handling or device control protocol such as Megaco (H.248), SIP or MGCP to pass along the information needed to set up ATM and AAL2 bearer connections. The connections can carry voice, voiceband data, clear channel circuit emulation, video and baseband data such as fax relay, modem relay, SSCOP or frame relay.

The RFC keeps to standard SDP syntax from RFC 2327. It extends the values of existing fields instead of defining new fields, and only the media attribute lines get new attributes. Because the network type is set to ATM, a standard SDP parser should not misread the extended values. Parameters for layers above the adaptation layer are included only when they are tightly coupled to the ATM or AAL layers.

It covers new SVCs set up per service connection, and existing resources such as PVCs, SPVCs, cached SVCs or CIDs inside AAL2 connections that are assigned to a service connection. It does not address SDP for IP, with or without ATM below it. The RFC says the list of conventions is meant to be exhaustive, and that individual applications can use subsets.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a standard order form for renting a phone line on an old network. This RFC says how to fill in that form so every company reads it the same way.

sections.title: Writing Values: Wildcards, Directions and Case
sections.content:
Parameters are written in decimal, in hexadecimal, as strings, or in either number format. When both are possible a 0x prefix marks hex. Leading zeros are not used in decimal, and parsers must not reject leading zeros in hex values. String values are enclosed in double quotes.

Two special characters stand in for values. A $ is a wildcard that lets the recipient pick any permitted value. A dash (hyphen) says the value is not needed because it is irrelevant or known from provisioning, defaults, another protocol or another part of the descriptor. If these characters are felt to break RFC 2327 syntax, the strings CHOOSE and OMIT may be used instead.

The RFC fixes the meaning of forward and backward. Forward means away from the ATM node under consideration and backward means towards it, no matter which side started the connection. ATM signaling uses the opposite idea, where forward runs from the side that initiates set-up, so a gateway may have to swap the two.

SDP syntax is case-sensitive, so these conventions are too, although parsers are encouraged to be case-tolerant where no ambiguity results. New attributes are written without the X- prefix for legibility, while codec names not registered with IANA do use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has a few shortcuts. A dollar sign means "you pick" and a dash means "not needed here". Forward just means "away from me" and backward means "towards me".

sections.title: Shape of an ATM Session Description
sections.content:
An ATM session description is a session-level part followed by one or two media-level parts. The two media are the ATM bearer and, where applicable, RTCP control. The session part uses the lines v, o, s, c, b, t and k, and carries no media attribute lines. The ATM bearer media part has an m line, optional b and k lines, and any number of a lines.

The v, o, s and t lines are generally mandatory, but in the Megaco context they are optional and most MGCP applications omit o, s and t. The protocol version is 0. Parsers are encouraged not to reject descriptions that lack these lines.

On the origin line the user name is a single hyphen, the session ID is an NTP-style timestamp or a call, connection or context ID, and the network type is ATM or a wildcard. The session name is always s= followed by a hyphen. The stop time on the t line is set to 0. The RFC says that encryption of ATM and AAL2 bearers, and of their signaling, has not yet been conventionalized.
sections.plainLanguage: Every description has the same few lines in the same order, a bit like a form with a header and then a section about the actual line. Some boxes are always filled with a dash because they do not matter here.

sections.title: ATM Addresses and Connection Identifiers
sections.content:
The connection line is c=<networkType> <addressType> <address>. For ATM the address type can be NSAP, E164 or GWID (also written ALIAS). An NSAP address is 40 hex digits in dotted form, an E.164 address is a decimal number of up to 15 digits, and a gateway identifier is an alphanumeric string that should fit in 32 characters. Any field on the line may be wildcarded, but a field must not be left out.

The media line carries a virtual connection ID in the place of the port. It is built from labelled pieces such as VCCI-, VPCI-, VPI-, VCI-, PORT-, BCG- and CID-, joined with slashes. Examples are VCCI-27 for a whole virtual circuit and VCCI-40/CID-$ for a wildcarded channel inside one. The VPI is 8 or 12 bits, the VCI is 16 bits and the CID is 8 bits. A bearer connection group bundles up to 255 VPCs or VCCs.

The VCCI and VPCI keep their value across crossconnects and are normally unique between a pair of nodes. When both ends can assign them, the RFC suggests reducing glare by taking values from opposite ends of the range.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses are like street addresses for gateways, and the connection ID is like an apartment number inside the building. You can write a dollar sign instead and let the other side choose a free apartment.

sections.title: The Media Line: Transport and Format List
sections.content:
The media line is m=<media> <virtualConnectionId> <transport> <format list>. The media is one of the values from RFC 2327. The transport names how the service payload is encapsulated, and the RFC points to other documents for the details: values such as AAL1/ATMF, AAL5/ITU, AAL2/ATMF and AAL2/ITU refer to ATM Forum or ITU-T specifications. Custom values like AAL2/custom, a corporate name, or an IEEE OUI mark non-standard schemes that must be used consistently within a deployment. H.323 Annex C uses RTP/AVP.

For AAL1 and AAL5, the format list is a list of RTP payload types, usually in order of preference. The numbers 0 to 95 are static and listed with IANA, and encodings without a static number are mapped dynamically in the range 96 to 127 using the atmmap attribute. For AAL2, the format list is a list of profile numbers from 1 to 255, and the line can hold several transport and profile list pairs.

Where a value is not needed it is replaced by a hyphen. Data media use forms such as m=data <virtualConnectionId> followed by two hyphens, with attribute lines saying how the data is adapted. For example, an sbc attribute gives the subchannel count for n x 64 circuit emulation.
sections.plainLanguage: This line says what kind of thing is being sent, which road it will use, and a ranked list of the ways it could be packed. The first choice goes first, like picking a favourite flavour and then some backups.

sections.title: The Media Attributes
sections.content:
Most of the new vocabulary lives in a= lines, split into four groups. ATM bearer attributes describe the connection itself: eecid, aalType, capability (the transfer capability or service category such as CBR or rt-VBR), qosClass, bcob, stc, upcc, atmQOSparms, atmTrfcDesc, abrParms, abrSetup, bearerType, lij, anycast, cache and bearerSigIE.

AAL attributes such as aalApp, cbrRate, sbc, clkrec, fec, prtfl, structure, cpsSDUsize, aal2CPS, aal2sscs3661unassured, aal2sscs3661assured, aal2sscs3662 and aal5sscop describe the adaptation layer. Service attributes such as atmmap, silenceSupp, ecan, gc, profileDesc, vsel, dsel, fsel and onewaySel describe codecs and voice processing. A single miscellaneous attribute, chain, links consecutive descriptions that describe different layers of one connection.

Some are small and concrete. The bearerType attribute says whether the bearer is a PVC, an SVC or a CID, and optionally whether the gateway starts bearer signaling. The cache attribute enables SVC caching with an idle timer in seconds, so a=cache:on 7200 releases an SVC idle for 2 hours. The eecid attribute carries up to 8 hex digits. Attributes must not contradict each other or other lines, and inconsistencies are to be flagged as errors rather than ignored.

Some of these attributes, such as vsel, dsel and fsel, refer to codecs generically and can also be used for non-ATM sessions. The RFC advises against the RFC 2327 ptime attribute in ATM applications and says it should be flagged as an error for AAL1.
sections.plainLanguage: After the main line come lots of extra sticky notes. Each note answers one small question, like how fast, how reliable, or whether to turn on echo cancelling. You only stick on the notes you need.

sections.title: Using the eecid to Match Calls to Connections
sections.content:
The eecid (end-to-end connection identifier, called the bnc-id in Q.1901) correlates a service-level call with the bearer set-up request that carries it. Its value needs to be unique only within the node that terminates the SVC set-up. The RFC recommends keeping it until the connection ends.

The informative walk-through assumes bearer signaling that is independent of call control. In the backward model, the originating gateway offers its NSAP address and an eecid in SDP. The call controllers pass these along and the terminating gateway sets up an SVC to the originating one, putting the eecid in the Generic Information Transport information element. The originating gateway uses it to tie the SVC to the waiting call and replies with an SVC connect.

In the forward model the roles swap: the terminating gateway picks the eecid and the originating gateway sets up the SVC towards it. Either way, an SDP description with a=bearerType:SVC on tells a gateway that it is to initiate set-up. Other signaling carriers are mentioned too: a Q.2630.1 establish request can use the SUGR information element.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a claim ticket. One side hands out a ticket number, and when the other side calls to connect, it quotes the number so the first side knows which waiting call it belongs to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that standard encryption of ATM and AAL2 bearers is not conventionalized the way RTP payload encryption is, and neither is authentication of ATM or AAL2 bearer signaling. The SDP k= line from RFC 2327 can be used to represent an encryption key and the method of obtaining it.

It also warns that session descriptions may originate in untrusted areas such as subscriber premises. SDP relies on the security of the protocol that carries it (SIP, MGCP or Megaco) or of the layers below, and no additional mechanism is needed. Those protocols can use IPsec authentication as described in RFC 1826, with encryption optionally added.
sections.plainLanguage: The form does not lock anything by itself. If you want the message kept secret or checked, you rely on the envelope it travels in.

messages.note: Notifies the controller that the SVC is up.
